answer_json.answer: Fear is cutting your winners short

lesson_text: Fear is cutting your winners short. The emotion field says anxious on 7 of 8 early exits, and each stock went on to hit your target. Steenbarger calls worry and nervousness clues to track. Once you see a fear pattern, you can work on it. A report for the SEC describes the disposition effect: investors tend to sell winning positions and hold onto losing ones. Odean found it widespread and counterproductive. A planned sale is not this. A sale out of fear, before your plan, is. Same feeling on the same mistake is a pattern. The emotion field is how you find it.

facts.given: Trade A risked $200 and made $500. Trade B risked $1,000 and made $1,500. Which did better for its risk? Trade A, it made 2.5x its risk Trade B, it made $1,500 in all Neither, the sizes differ too much Can't tell without the win rate

reveal_json.lesson_line: Log every result in R. Then a small trade and a big one compare fairly.
reveal_json.simple: Trade A did better, because it made 2.5 times the money it put at risk.
reveal_json.why: Trade A, at 2.5R. R is the risk you took at entry, and Tharp says to read every profit and loss as a multiple of it. $500 on $200 of risk is 2.5R. Trade B made $1,500, but it put $1,000 at risk to get it, so it earned less per dollar risked. In R, a small trade and a big one compare fairly. This does not make B a bad trade. A simply paid more per dollar risked.

wrong.Can't tell without the win rate: Win rate is the share of closed trades that make money. One trade's result is read in R: its gain over its risk.
wrong.Neither, the sizes differ too much: That's exactly what R fixes. Dividing by the risk puts both trades on the same scale.
wrong.Trade B, it made $1,500 in all: More dollars, but on a much bigger risk. Per dollar risked, B earned less than A.

lesson_text: Write a daily trade cap and keep it. It names one action, and next Sunday you can check whether you kept it. Steenbarger's test for a plan is what, specifically, you will do. Thin extended-hours trading usually means wider spreads, or no quotes at all. Many brokers take only limit orders outside regular hours, to protect you from bad prices. With fewer buyers and sellers outside regular hours, an order may fill only in part, or not at all. Thin extended-hours trading can leave an order unfilled or fill it at a worse price. News released outside regular hours can move a stock sharply before the next open. List what would change your mind when you place the trade, so you keep a clear head later.
